message of his holiness pope leo xiv for the 100th world mission day 2026 18 october 2026. 3. mission to love – proclaiming, living and sharing god’s faithful love. if unity is the condition of mission, love is its essence. the good news that we are sent to proclaim to the world is not an abstract ideal; it is the gospel of god’s faithful love, which became flesh in the face and life of jesus christ. the mission of the disciples and the church as a whole is to continue the mission of christ in the holy spirit: a mission born of love, lived in love, and leading to love. in fact, the lord himself, in his great prayer to the father before his passion, after invoking unity among his disciples, concludes: “so that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and i in them” (jn 17:26). impelled by the love of christ, the apostles then went out to evangelize for christ (cf. 2 cor 5:14). in the same way, throughout the centuries, multitudes of christians — martyrs, confessors and missionaries — have given their lives to make this divine love known to the world. thus, guided by the holy spirit, the spirit of love, the church’s evangelizing mission will continue until the end of time. i would like to express my special gratitude to today’s ad gentes missionaries. like saint francis xavier, they have left their homeland, their families and all sense of security in order to proclaim the gospel and bring christ and his love to places that are often challenging, poor, conflict-ridden or culturally distant. despite adversity and human limitations, they continue to give themselves joyfully, because they know that christ himself, and his gospel, are the greatest treasures we can offer. through their perseverance, they demonstrate that god’s love transcends all barriers. the world still needs these courageous witnesses of christ, and ecclesial communities still need new missionary vocations. we must always keep them close to our hearts and continually pray to the father for them. may he grant us the gift of young people and adults who are willing to leave everything behind to follow christ on the path of evangelization even to the ends of the earth! filled with admiration for men and women missionaries, i make a special appeal to the whole church to join them in the mission of evangelization through the witness of our lives in christ, through prayer and through our contributions to the missions. as saint francis of assisi said, “love is not loved,” and we look to him in a special way on the eight hundredth anniversary of his passing to heaven. let us find inspiration in his desire to live in the love of the lord and to transmit it to those both near and far, because, as he said, “this love who hath loved us much is much to be loved” (saint bonaventure of bagnoregio, the life of saint francis, chap. ix, 1; fonti francescane, 1161). let us also draw inspiration from the zeal of saint thérèse of the child jesus, who declared that she would continue her mission even after death: “i shall desire in heaven the same thing as i do now on earth: to love jesus and to make him loved” (letter 220 to l’abbé bellière, 24 february 1897). inspired by these testimonies, let us all commit to contributing to the great mission of evangelization — which is always a work of love —according to our own vocation and the gifts we have received. your prayers and practical support, particularly on world mission day, will be a great help in bringing the gospel of god’s love to everyone, especially the poorest and those most in need. every gift, no matter how small, becomes a meaningful act of missionary communion. i renew my heartfelt gratitude “for everything you will do to help me help missionaries throughout the world” (video message for world mission day 2025, 19 october 2025). to foster spiritual communion, i give you my blessing with this simple prayer: holy father, make us one in christ, rooted in his love that unites and renews. may all members of the church be united in mission, docile to the holy spirit, courageous in bearing witness to the gospel, proclaiming and daily embodying your faithful love for all creatures. bless all missionary men and women, support them in their efforts, and watch over them in hope! mary, queen of missions, accompany our work of evangelization in every corner of the earth: make us instruments of peace, and grant that the whole world may recognize in christ the light that saves. amen. *st mary’s annual christmas blitz will be held from december 26th to 30th 2026 this sunday is world mission sunday october is designated as mission month. there are approximately 1,300 irish born missionaries working in more than 80 countries around the world. during this month we unite ourselves in prayer with them and the communities with whom they serve. a special diocesan collection will be held this weekend. a report on pope leo’s short video message in english for this mission sunday world mission sunday is held every year on the second-to-last sunday of oct ober. this year it will take place on 18th october with the theme of “missionaries of hope among the peoples.” "iurge every catholic parish in the world to take part in world mission sunday," insisted pope leo xiv in a video message for the occasion of world mission sunday. the video begins with the holy father recalling that on world mission sunday every year, the whole church prays, united, particularly for missionaries and the fruitfulness of their apostol ic labours. "when i served as a missionary priest and bishop in peru," pope leo illustrated, "i saw first- hand how the faith, the prayer and the generosity shown on world mission sunday can transform entire communit ies." "i urge every catholic parish in the world to take part in world mission sunday," pope leo said, underscoring, "your prayers, your financial support will help spread the gospel , provide for pastoral and catechetical programs, help to build new churches, and care for the health and educational needs of our brothers and sisters in mission territories." "this october 18th, as we reflect together on our baptismal call to be “missionaries of the peoples," the pope encouraged, "let us commit ourselves anew to the sweet and joyful task of bringing christ jesus our hope to the ends of the earth." the holy father concluded by thanking parishes worldwide for everything they do to help him to help missionaries throughout the world and imparting his apostolic blessing . tarbert active retirement – (over 55’s) meet in tarbert bridewell every friday between 10.30am and 12 noon. we have different activities every week followed by refreshments. new members are welcome. clothes collection – the shannonside women’s group will hold a clothes collection in church car park on friday 30th oct. from 8am until 10.30am. bags can also be dropped off at the tarbert community centre on thursday 29th oct. from 6pm to 7pm. the proceeds are going to kerry hospice / palliative care and health lin k / transport. thank you – a total of €876.75 was raised at the kerry hospice foundation coffee morning held at the tarbert bridewell. a huge thank you to all involved and who made it such a special morning. youth ministry in the diocese of kerry - the diocesan springs of hope newsletter is now available to view. the newsletter provides a colourful and interesting look at some of the exciting things hap pening within the diocese of kerry in the area of youth ministry and the people involved. so, grab a cuppa and have a read! can access this by going directly to

a note from fr. over the past twenty years, ireland has undergone an extraordinary transformation. we have moved from a society deeply rooted in christianity to one increasingly shaped by secular values. as one english commentator recently remarked, ireland has gone from organising itself around the catholic religion to organising itself around the “woke religion." we see this in changing attitudes towards the sacredness of human life, marriage, family and the place of christianity in public life. there was a time when people looked to the gospel, the 10 commandments and the teachings of the church as their moral compass. today, many look instead to politicians, legislators and the laws of the land. the assumption seems to be that if something is legal, it must be morally right. but since when did a majority vote determine what is good or evil? let us not forget nazi germany, where appalling injustices were given the force of law and accepted or tolerated by so many. history reminds us that something can be perfectly legal and yet profoundly immoral. the law of the land is not necessarily the law of god. in this sunday's gospel, jesus tells us: “give back to caesar what belongs to caesar and to god what belongs to god." jesus asks for a coin: “whose image is this?" “caesar's,” they reply. but there is a deeper question. if the coin bears caesar's image, whose image do you and i bear? genesis gives us the answer: we are created in the image and likeness of god. jesus is not telling us to disregard civil authority. we have a christian responsibility to be good citizens, pay our taxes, respect just laws and contribute to the common good. but caesar is not god. governments have legitimate authority, but that authority has limits. when the laws of the state conflict with god's law, our first allegiance must always be to god. as st peter reminds us,“we must obey god rather than men." the coin belongs to caesar because it bears his image. but we belong to god because we bear his image. god doesn't simply want an hour on sunday or a few prayers. he wants our hearts, our minds and our whole lives. perhaps that is the real challenge of today's gospel: who ultimately governs my life? caesar, with his changing laws and values, or god, whose truth never changes? so who do i belong to caesar? (our government) or do i belong to god? give caesar what is rightly his, but never give caesar what belongs to god.

there are some weeks when the gospel seems to meet us exactly where we are. this is one of those weeks. over recent days, many of us have been shocked and de eply disturbed by the loss of live of four members of a family in waterford. i n times like these, people can find themselves searching for answers and struggling to understand why suffering occurs. in the face of such evil and suffering, many people ask difficult questions. where was god?how can something so terrible happen? how are we me ant to make sense of such cruelty? these are not new questions. they are questions that faithful people have asked for centuries. even jesus , hanging on the cross, cried out in anguish. faith does not remove pain, nor does it provide simple answers to life's darkest moments. the gospel today reminds us that we live in this world, but we belong ultimately to god. yet our world often feels overwhelmed by fea r, violence, anger, and division. many people are carrying anxieties about their families, their future, and the safety of their communities. we are more connect ed than ever through television, smartphones, and social media, yet many people feel more worried, isolated, and burdened than ever before. part of the challenge is what many call "information overload." within minutes of a tragedy occurring, we are inundated with images, c ommentary, speculation, and endless updates. while it is important to stay infor med, there comes a point when constant exposure to distressing news begins to weigh heavily on our minds and spirits. we find ourselves absorbing fear that we do little about. as christians, we are not called to ignore the suffe ring of the world. we are called to pray, to care, and to act where we can. but neithe r are we called to carry the weight of every tragedy alone. sometimes caring for our spiritual wellbeing means stepping away from the endless news cycle, tur ning off our phones for a while, spending time with family, taking a walk, pr aying quietly, or simply sitting in god's presence. continued back page… st. colman’s parish 29th sunday in ordinary time 17th/18th october 2026 milltown

in today's gospel from matthew jesus faces the first challenge to his teachings from the pharisees. they failed to see jesus as the word of god, the love of god and the power of god. all they saw was someone breaking their laws. they tried to trap jesus into saying something with which they could condemn him. a delegation composed of pharisees who hated rome and some herodians who worked with rome approached jesus with a question. both sides hated each other but their hatred of jesus united them. they open their conversation flattering jesus for his honesty and sense of justice. jesus saw through their hypocrisy at once. they then posed the question : "tell us then, what you think. is it lawful to pay taxes to caesar or not? this question put jesus in a difficult position as the pharisees did not want to pay taxes to the romans while the herodians were willing to pay taxes. jesus knows that the answer to the question is not what the group is interested in rather they want to trap jesus into a yes or no answer which would alienate one or other section of the community against him. jesus asks them to show him a coin. on the coin is the head of caesar. jesus answers their question "give therefore to caesar the things that are caesar's and to god the things that are god's.” in some ways we are people of this world and also of jesus. our loyalties as christians are first to god and then trying to make the world a better place through living as witnesses of god's word. there can be times when there is conflict, we can’t allow our loyalty to earthly goods ever to overcome our loyalty to god. where there's disrespect for life, injustice, war, racism, or any other evils in our society our loyalty to god moves us to speak and work to alleviate such things. we are obliged to be positive and speak the truth in love. since god’s image is stamped on each baptized person he or she is owned by him and so must give himself or herself to him. as st. thomas more said "the king’s good servant, but god's first.

a sst. crohan’s church, caherdaniel; chtwey & mary immact month of prayer for vocations to the priesthood untying the rope: the courage to begin . throughout october, our diocese is dedicating a month to prayer for vocations to the diocesan priesthood in kerry. each week invites us to reflect on a different aspect of the journey. this week, our theme is “setting sail” — a special invitation to those who may be discerning god's call to the priesthood. our thoughts turn naturally to st brendan the navigator, our great kerry saint, who reminds us that every journey begins with a willingness to leave the familiar behind. brendan did not remain on the shore, waiting until every uncertainty had been resolved. he untied the rope, set sail and entrusted himself to god. there is something deeply meaningful in that image for anyone discerning a vocation. it can be tempting to wait until we have all the answers, until the whole journey is mapped out, or until we feel completely ready. yet god rarely reveals the entire voyage at once. he invites us to trust him enough to take the next faithful step. is god calling you? an invitation to men in our parish and throughout south kerry if you have ever wondered whether god might be calling you to the diocesan priesthood, please do not be afraid to take that first step. reach out to fr sean or your local priest. you will be met with understanding, encouragement and every support as you explore what god may be asking of you. there is no need to have everything figured out before beginning the conversation. discerning is a journey, and you do not have to make it alone. you may be surprised by where that first conversation leads. all that is asked at the beginning is a willing heart and the courage to listen.

the evil we witness can tempt us to despair, but de spair is never the christian response. our response is hope. not a naïve hope that ignores reality, but a hope rooted in the belief that goodness is stronger than hatred, light is stronger than darkness, and love is stronger than death. perhaps this week's tragedy reminds us of what truly matters. life is precious and fragile. the arguments, jealousies, resentments , and worries that consume so much of our energy suddenly seem less important. what remains important are the relationships we nurture, the kindness we show , and the love we share with those closest to us. as we gather for mass this weekend, let us pray for all affected by the tragedy in waterford, for those who live in fear, for emerge ncy responders, and for all who struggle to find hope in difficult times. may go d help us to be people of peace in an anxious world, people of compassion in a hurting world, and people of hope in a world that desperately needs it. lord of all compassion, we pray for all of those caught up in the midst of tragedy. for those who have lost life and those working to save life. for those who are worried for people they love. for those who will see their loved ones no longer. for those in need of the peace that passes all understanding. for all who turn to you in the midst of turmoil. for those who cry out to you in fear and in love. for those in confusion and those in despair. for those whose tears are yet to dry. for those in need of your unending love. amen. last weekend’s offertory collection: €990.00 thank you for your generosity and continued support! killorglin pastoral area priest on duty this weekend kevin sullivan (087) 6277 638
